title: What is React?
summary: **React** is a declarative, component-based JavaScript library for building user interfaces. You describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React efficiently updates the DOM to match.

subtopics.title: Declarative UI
subtopics.explanation: Declarative UI means you describe what the screen should look like for a given state, and React figures out how to get there, rather than writing step-by-step instructions to mutate the DOM. This matters because it removes a whole class of bugs where the UI and data drift apart — you only ever update the data, and the UI follows. It works because React treats your component's return value as a description (UI = f(state)) and re-derives the screen whenever state changes.

subtopics.title: Components
subtopics.explanation: Components are the building blocks of React — small, reusable, self-contained functions that return a description of a piece of UI. They matter because they let you split a complex interface into independent pieces you can build, test, and reuse in isolation. A React app is a tree of components, each owning its own markup and logic, composed together like nested HTML elements.

subtopics.title: Virtual DOM
subtopics.explanation: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight in-memory representation of the UI that React keeps in JavaScript. When state changes, React builds a new virtual tree and compares it to the previous one, then applies only the minimal set of real DOM mutations needed. It matters because direct DOM manipulation is expensive and error-prone; the Virtual DOM lets React batch and minimize updates while you write simple declarative code. Note its value is predictable, maintainable updates at scale — not necessarily raw speed over hand-tuned vanilla JS.

subtopics.title: One-way data flow
subtopics.explanation: In React, data flows in a single direction — downward from parent to child through props. This matters because it makes data movement predictable: you can always trace where a value came from and what will re-render when it changes. Children never write directly to their props; instead they signal changes upward by calling callback functions the parent passed down, keeping a single source of truth.

subtopics.title: Reconciliation
subtopics.explanation: Reconciliation is the diffing process React uses to figure out what actually changed between the previous render and the new one. When state updates, React compares the new element tree against the old one and computes the smallest set of real DOM operations to apply. It matters because it is what makes declarative rendering efficient — you re-describe the whole UI on every render, but React only touches the nodes that genuinely differ.

subtopics.title: Library vs framework
subtopics.explanation: React is a focused UI library, not a full framework like Angular. It deliberately handles only the view layer, leaving routing, data fetching, and global state to separate tools you choose (React Router, Next.js, Redux, etc.). This matters in interviews because it explains React's flexibility and why it's often paired with a meta-framework like Next.js — you assemble your own stack rather than getting one prescribed.

foundations.overview: React is a library (not a full framework) for building user interfaces out of small, reusable pieces called components. Instead of manually finding DOM nodes and updating them step by step, you describe the UI as a function of your data, and React figures out the minimal set of DOM changes needed to keep the screen in sync.
foundations.formalDefinition: React is an open-source JavaScript library, created and maintained by Meta, for building composable user interfaces using a declarative programming model. Components return a description of the UI (typically written in JSX); React reconciles that description against the current UI and applies the necessary updates to the host environment (the DOM in browsers).
foundations.whyItMatters: React reframed UI development around state. Rather than imperatively mutating the DOM as events happen, you keep state in one place and let React derive the UI from it. This eliminates a whole class of bugs where the screen and the data drift out of sync, and it scales from a single widget to applications with thousands of components.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of your UI as a pure function: UI = f(state). When the state changes, you re-run the function to get a new description of the UI, and React works out the difference between the old and new descriptions, touching only the parts of the DOM that actually changed.
foundations.browserPerspective: In the browser, React keeps a lightweight in-memory representation of the UI (the Virtual DOM / fiber tree). When state changes, React builds a new tree, diffs it against the previous one (reconciliation), and then makes the smallest possible set of real DOM mutations. The browser only repaints the nodes that genuinely changed, which is far cheaper than rebuilding everything.
foundations.realWorldUsage: React powers Facebook, Instagram, Netflix's UI, Airbnb, and countless dashboards, e-commerce sites, and internal tools. It is also the foundation for meta-frameworks like Next.js and Remix, and for React Native, which renders to native mobile views instead of the DOM.
foundations.businessImpact: React's component model lets teams ship features faster by reusing UI pieces and reasoning about each component in isolation. Its huge ecosystem and talent pool reduce hiring and onboarding costs, which is why it is the default choice for many product teams.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Declarative, component-based code is easier to test, reason about, and refactor than imperative DOM manipulation. One-way data flow makes data movement predictable, so engineers can trace where a value comes from and what re-renders when it changes.
foundations.performanceImpact: React's diffing avoids unnecessary DOM work, but the Virtual DOM is not free — re-rendering large trees or doing heavy work in render can cause jank. Understanding when components re-render is key to keeping React apps fast.
commonUseCases: Single-page applications (SPAs) with rich, stateful UIs
Reusable design-system components shared across a product
Dashboards and admin panels that update as data changes
Server-rendered apps via meta-frameworks like Next.js

commonMisconceptions.myth: React is a full framework like Angular.
commonMisconceptions.reality: React is a focused UI library. Routing, data fetching, and state management are handled by separate libraries you choose, which is why React is often paired with tools like React Router or Next.js.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The Virtual DOM makes React faster than plain DOM manipulation.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Hand-tuned vanilla JS can be faster in micro-benchmarks. The Virtual DOM's value is predictable, maintainable updates at scale — not raw speed.

visualExplorer.title: The component tree
visualExplorer.caption: A React app is a tree of components. Data flows down through props from parent to child — explore how the pieces nest together.

interactiveExamples.title: Declarative UI from state
interactiveExamples.explanation: Notice you never touch the DOM directly. You hold a value in state and describe what the UI should look like for that value; React updates the screen when the value changes.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A heading and a button. Clicking the button toggles both the heading text and the button label.

interactiveExamples.title: Composing components
interactiveExamples.explanation: A React UI is built from components that nest inside one another, just like HTML elements. Here App renders two Greeting components, each customised with a prop.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A heading followed by two greeting lines, one for Ada and one for Linus.

codeLab.title: Render a value declaratively
codeLab.instructions: Create a component that holds a name in state and renders 'Welcome, <name>' in an <h2>. Add a button that changes the name to 'World' when clicked. Do not touch the DOM directly — let React render from state.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A heading that reads 'Welcome, World' after the button is clicked.
hints: Hold the name in useState so React re-renders when it changes.
Read the state value inside the JSX with {name} instead of writing to the DOM.

debuggingLab.title: Manually mutating the DOM in React
debuggingLab.symptom: The counter on screen never updates even though the variable is being incremented.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: React re-renders a component only when its state or props change. A plain local variable like count is reset to 0 on every render and never tells React to update, so the UI is frozen at the initial value.
commonMistakes: Using a regular variable to track changing values instead of state.
Expecting React to notice changes you make outside of its state/props system.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make the count live in React state so changing it triggers a re-render.

theory.question: What is React and why was it created?
theory.directAnswer: React is a declarative, component-based JavaScript library for building user interfaces, created by Meta. It lets you describe the UI as a function of state, and it efficiently updates the DOM to match using a Virtual DOM and reconciliation.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A library for composing UIs from reusable components that render based on their current state and props.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Manually keeping the DOM in sync with changing data is error-prone and hard to scale. React was created to let developers describe the desired UI declaratively and let the library handle the updates.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Components return a description of the UI. React builds an in-memory tree, diffs it against the previous one when state changes, and applies the minimal set of real DOM mutations.

theory.whyImportant: Understanding React's core purpose — declarative, component-based UI — frames everything else you learn, so interviewers open with it to gauge your foundations.
theory.realWorldExample: Facebook's news feed updates pieces of the page as new data arrives without you writing manual DOM updates for each change.

nestedTopics.title: Declarative vs imperative
nestedTopics.explanation: Declarative code describes the end state ('show this list'); imperative code lists the steps ('create node, append, set text').

nestedTopics.title: Library vs framework
nestedTopics.explanation: React focuses on the view layer; routing and data fetching come from other libraries you choose.

nestedTopics.title: Component model
nestedTopics.explanation: UIs are built from small, reusable, composable components that own their own logic and markup.

followUps.question: Is React a framework?
followUps.answer: No — it's a UI library. It deliberately leaves routing, data fetching, and global state to other tools, which gives flexibility but means you assemble your own stack.

followUps.question: Who maintains React?
followUps.answer: React is open source, created and maintained primarily by Meta along with a large community of contributors.

scenario.question: A teammate built a small interactive widget in vanilla JavaScript and keeps fighting bugs where the screen and the underlying data disagree. Why might React help, and what is the core shift in approach?
scenario.directAnswer: Those bugs come from imperatively mutating the DOM in many places, so the data and the UI drift apart. React fixes this by making the UI a declarative function of a single source of truth: you update state, and React derives the entire UI from it, so the screen can't silently fall out of sync.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A move from manually patching the DOM (imperative) to describing the UI for a given state (declarative).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Hand-written DOM updates scatter the 'truth' across event handlers, making it easy to update one place and forget another.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: With React, state is the single source of truth. Every render recomputes the UI from state, and React reconciles the difference, so there is only one place that determines what is on screen.

scenario.whyImportant: This 'UI = f(state)' insight is the central reason teams adopt React, and explaining it shows you understand the value, not just the syntax.

nestedTopics.title: Single source of truth
nestedTopics.explanation: State lives in one place; the UI is always derived from it rather than edited independently.

nestedTopics.title: One-way data flow
nestedTopics.explanation: Data flows down from parent to child via props, making it easy to trace where values come from.

followUps.question: When might vanilla JS still be the better choice?
followUps.answer: For a tiny, mostly static page or a single trivial widget, React's bundle and tooling overhead may not be worth it.

coding.question: Build a simple component that shows a message and a button; clicking the button switches the message between 'Off' and 'On'.
coding.thoughtProcess: I need a piece of state to remember whether it's on or off, and a button whose click handler flips that state. The displayed text is derived from the state, so I just read it during render rather than storing the text separately.
coding.lineByLine: useState(false) creates the boolean state. The <h2> reads the state and shows 'On' or 'Off'. The button's onClick flips the boolean with the functional updater setOn(o => !o), which triggers a re-render so the UI updates declaratively.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) per click for the state update.

alternativeApproaches.title: Vanilla JS toggle
alternativeApproaches.explanation: You could query the elements and manually set textContent on each click, but you'd be responsible for keeping every part of the UI in sync yourself.

followUps.question: Why not store the displayed text ('On'/'Off') in state too?
followUps.answer: It's derived from the boolean, so computing it during render keeps a single source of truth and avoids the two values getting out of sync.

productionDeepDive.architecture: A React app is structured as a tree of components rooted at a single component (often <App />) mounted into one DOM node. Larger apps layer routing, data fetching, and shared state around that tree, but the component tree remains the backbone of the architecture.
productionDeepDive.performance: React avoids unnecessary DOM work via reconciliation, but rendering large trees or doing heavy computation in render can still cause jank. In production you measure with the React Profiler and split or memoize components so state changes re-render the smallest possible subtree.
productionDeepDive.security: React escapes values rendered in JSX by default, which mitigates many XSS attacks. The main risk is dangerouslySetInnerHTML — only use it with sanitized content. Never trust client-side state for authorization decisions.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As apps grow, teams adopt conventions for folder structure, a design system of shared components, and a meta-framework like Next.js for routing and rendering. Code splitting keeps the initial bundle small as the number of components grows.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: The component model encourages small, single-responsibility pieces that are easy to test and reuse. One-way data flow makes it straightforward to trace where data originates and what re-renders when it changes.
productionDeepDive.observability: React DevTools lets you inspect the component tree, props, and state in a running app, and highlight re-renders. Error boundaries catch render errors and report them to monitoring tools.

caseStudies.problem: Keeping a constantly updating, deeply interactive feed in sync with data using manual DOM updates was bug-prone and hard to scale across many engineers.
caseStudies.solution: Built React so the UI is a declarative function of state, with a Virtual DOM that reconciles changes efficiently.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Added a build step and a runtime library in exchange for predictable, maintainable UI code.
caseStudies.lessons: Declarative, component-based UI scales to large teams and complex, frequently changing interfaces far better than ad-hoc DOM manipulation.

projectBuilder.summary: Lay the foundation of the dashboard by scaffolding the root component tree and rendering a static layout declaratively from data.
requirements: A root App component that renders the dashboard shell
A reusable StatCard component used several times with different props
A header and a content area composed from smaller components
projectBuilder.architecture: Create an App component as the root of the tree. Break the UI into a Header component and a content area that maps over an array of stats to render StatCard components, passing data down via props.

steps.title: Scaffold the root component
steps.instructions: Create an App component that returns the overall layout div and a Header.
steps.checkpoint: The app renders a header at the top of the page.

steps.title: Build a reusable StatCard
steps.instructions: Create a StatCard component that takes label and value props and renders them.
steps.checkpoint: A single StatCard renders with the data you pass it.

steps.title: Render cards from data
steps.instructions: Map over an array of stat objects in App and render a StatCard for each.
steps.checkpoint: Several cards appear, each driven by data rather than hard-coded markup.

enhancements: Add a loading state before the stats appear
Extract the layout into a reusable DashboardShell component
interviewQuestions: Why is rendering cards from a data array preferable to hard-coding each card?
How does one-way data flow show up in this component tree?

keyTakeaways: React is a declarative, component-based library for building user interfaces.
You describe the UI as a function of state (UI = f(state)); React updates the DOM to match.
Components compose into a tree, and data flows one way — down via props.
The Virtual DOM and reconciliation let React apply minimal, efficient DOM updates.
React is a focused UI library, not a full framework — you choose tools for routing and data.
